Earlier this week, Novo Nordisk ended its partnership with the telehealth store Hims & Hers Health. This allowed Hims to sell the Novo weight loss drug Wegovy at a lower price for cash-paying patients.

The feud between the two companies, which sent Hims shares down more than 30% on Monday, is just the latest disruption for patients looking to lose weight using GLP-1 drugs sold by Novo and its rival, Eli Lilly.

The huge growth last year of the market for legal knockoff weight loss drugs caused huge problems for Novo and Lilly. They had seen big gains in market value amid the hype that had greeted the launch of their respective obesity blockbusters, Wegovy and Zepbound.

By early 2025, both stocks had pulled back amid a broader reconsideration of the weight loss opportunity.

Today, the legal knockoffs are mostly gone, but the market for the weight loss drugs is still in turmoil. Here’s what you need to know about the weight loss drug market now, and where it’s headed.

Why can’t you buy compounded semaglutide anymore?

When a branded drug is in short supply in the U.S., compounding pharmacies are allowed to make and sell knockoff versions. That’s usually not a big deal for pharmaceutical companies, but the prolonged shortages of Zepbound and Wegovy — combined with massive demand — created an opportunity that the rising telehealth industry seized.

Companies like Hims & Hers, Ro, Noom, and other smaller competitors jumped into the compounded semaglutide market last year, selling the legal knockoff drugs at prices generally starting around $200 for the first month of treatment, and $300 per month as dosage levels increase. That was a huge discount to Wegovy’s list price of $1,350 per month, and consumers leaped at the opportunity to get a cheaper version of a GLP-1 weight loss drug.

Novo believes that over a million people were taking compounded GLP-1 drugs by early 2025.

When the Food and Drug Administration declared that the shortages of Zepbound and Wegovy were over, they set a deadline for compounding pharmacies to stop making semaglutide in bulk. That deadline passed on May 22nd. Since then, the compounding pharmacies that supply telehealth firms haven’t been allowed to make compounded semaglutide to sell on a large scale.

What are the options for patients?

For patients whose insurance covers Zepbound or Wegovy, nothing has changed.

But for the patients without coverage who lost access to compounded semaglutide as of late May, Lilly and Novo offered an alternative: cash-pay options for Wegovy and Zepbound that are cheaper than the list price, but more expensive than the compounded versions.

Novo’s direct-to-consumer offering comes in an injector pen just like the version that patients get through regular pharmacy channels, while Lilly’s direct-to-consumer Zepbound comes in a vial that patients need to draw and inject themselves.

Through its in-house online pharmacy, Novo sells Wegovy to patients without insurance coverage for $499 per month. (It’s currently running a special offer for a month of Wegovy for $199.) Lilly, through its own online pharmacy, sells Zepbound for $499 per month for most dosage levels, and $349 per month for the starter dose.

Both Novo and Lilly have set up partnerships that allow some of the telehealth firms that sold compounded GLP-1s to offer the cheaper direct-to-consumer version of their branded weight loss shots. Novo announced arrangements with Hims, LifeMD, and Ro in April, while Teladoc Health and LifeMD have access to Lilly’s pharmacy.

The partnership between Hims and Novo caused a stir early this week, sending Hims shares plummeting.

Why are some telehealth pharmacies still selling compounded semaglutide?

You can still easily find online pharmacies advertising compounded semaglutide. Hims, for example, is advertising “personalized compounded GLP-1” injections for $165 per month for patients who pay for a full year upfront.

Compound pharmacies can’t make semaglutide in bulk anymore, but the U.S. law and FDA rules seem to let them make a prescription for a single patient under certain conditions.

The compounding semaglutide that’s still legal is probably sold as a personalized prescription that’s been tweaked in some way, making it different, maybe in dosage size, from the commercially available Wegovy. Weight loss jabs may achieve less drastic results outside trials, study suggests | Nicola Davis, The Guardian

Patients in real world shed less weight than in clinical settings and may benefit more from bariatric surgery

People using weight loss jabs shed far fewer pounds in the real world than in clinical trials, researchers have found.

Jabs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, which contain the drugs semaglutide and tirzepatide respectively, have transformed the treatment of obesity, with studies suggesting the former can help people lose up to 20% of their body weight after 72 weeks of treatment.

However, a new study suggests the drugs, known as GLP-1 RAs, may not produce such drastic weight loss in everyday settings.

“The average patient on [GLP-1 RAs] in the real world is not getting the weight loss that we see in clinical trials,” said the study’s senior author, Dr Karan Chhabra, from the Grossman school of medicine at New York University.

Researchers analysed data from 51,085 patients with a body mass index of 35 or greater and who were eligible for weight loss surgery and weight loss jabs.

The team compared the weight loss in 38,545 people prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide by their doctor with that in 12,540 patients who underwent weight loss surgery, over a period of up to three years.

After taking into account factors such as age, body mass index and health problems of participants, the team found patients who underwent bariatric surgery had significantly greater average weight loss at all measured time points than those who received prescriptions for semaglutide or tirzepatide.

For example, after two years, people who underwent bariatric surgery had on average a 26.5% reduction in their body weight, compared with 5.7% for those prescribed GLP-1 RAs for any duration.

The study has not yet been peer reviewed and is due to be presented at the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery 2025 annual scientific meeting.

Chhabra said: “The most reliable way to lose 20% to 30% of your weight is to get a bariatric operation.”

He said it was not clear why the weight loss jabs had a smaller effect in the real world than in trials, but he noted that their cost and others barriers to access could mean people were unable to continue their use over the long term, while doctors’ efforts could also play a role, given how it is important that dosage is increased over time, side-effects are monitored and additional support is offered.

Chhabra said further work was needed to ensure patients who want to take such medications get the greatest effectiveness.

“Our goal is to get as many people to the right treatment [for obesity] as possible. But they need to know what to expect from the treatment that they’re choosing, and that needs to be guided by real-world data, not clinical trial data,” he said.

'Ozempic Babies': Here's Why Oral Contraceptives Might Be Failing | Simon Cork, The Conversation

Weight loss drugs, including Wegovy (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide), are becoming increasingly popular among those trying to lose weight. But a rise in so-called "Ozempic babies" has led the UK's medicines regulator to issue guidance on their use by women of reproductive age.

The guidance comes after the agency received 40 reports of unintended pregnancies by women who had been using a weight loss drug. Of particular note is the effect that these drugs may have on the effectiveness of oral contraceptives.

Weight loss jabs (including both semaglutide and tirzepatide) act by mimicking the naturally occurring hormone GLP-1, which is released from the gut after we eat. One of the things this hormone helps to do is suppress appetite. Tirzepatide also acts on another naturally occurring hormone system called GIP, also known to suppress appetite.

The mechanism through which these drugs impact appetite is multifaceted. First, they inhibit regions of the brain associated with hunger. This suppresses the increase in appetite that occurs when people lose weight. GLP-1 drugs also slow how quickly food leaves the stomach.

There's currently very little published literature which has investigated the interactions between GLP-1 drugs and oral contraceptives. However, the effect these drugs have on stomach emptying appears to at least partly explain why the oral contraceptive pill may not work as well as expected.

One 2024 study demonstrated that tirzepatide reduced the amount of ethinylestradiol (a synthetic form of oestrogen, which is a component of the combined oral contraceptive pill) in the bloodstream by 20%. It also increased the amount of time it took the ethinylestradiol to be fully absorbed into the bloodstream by two to four hours.

This reduced absorbency hampers the drug's ability to suppress the action of the reproductive system in women. This will affect its contraceptive effects. Notably, the effects of semaglutide on ethinylestradiol absorption were less pronounced.

The increased length of time it took the contraceptive to be fully absorbed is probably a consequence of reduced gastric emptying since ethinylestradiol is primarily absorbed in the small intestine. The reasons why these effects were more pronounced in tirzepatide compared with semaglutide remain unclear.

However, one study showed that while both of these drugs affect gastric emptying to a similar degree, these effects are much longer lasting with tirzepatide.

Other possible factors
Two commonly observed side-effects of GLP-1 drugs include vomiting and diarrhoea – affecting 12% and 23% of patients taking tirzepatide respectively. Vomiting and diarrhoea have the potential to interfere with the absorption of all types of oral medications – including contraceptives.

This is because the drugs may be expelled from the body before they have an opportunity to be absorbed into the blood stream. People taking the contraceptive pill are advised to use a back-up contraceptive for this reason if they vomit or have diarrhoea to avoid unintended pregnancy.

Another factor that could explain the link between GLP-1 drug use and unintended pregnancy could be the effect that weight loss in general has on fertility.

Obesity has long been associated with reduced fertility. Obesity can also exacerbate other conditions which affect fertility – such as polycystic ovary syndrome, a hormonal disorder that affects how the ovaries work.

It is likely weight loss associated with taking GLP-1 drugs leads to an increase in fertility. This in turn could make women more likely to become pregnant – independent of whether they're using oral contraceptives or not.

So far, it doesn't appear that other forms of contraceptives are affected by GLP-1 weight loss drugs. Non-oral contraceptives, such as intrauterine devices (IUDs), transdermal patches and implants, are unlikely to be affected as their active ingredients are absorbed into the blood stream independently of the gastrointestinal tract. Likewise, physical barriers such as condoms and copper IUDs are also unaffected.

But women who use an oral contraceptive are advised to use an additional, non-oral form of contraception (such as condoms) for four weeks after starting semaglutide or tirzepatide. This is when side-effects are typically at their highest.

Because of a lack of evidence around the safety of these medications during pregnancy, women who do become pregnant while using a weight loss drug are advised to speak to their doctor to find alternative medications.

A New Obesity Pill May Burn Fat Without Suppressing Appetite | Emily Mullen, WIRED

An investigational drug developed by Eolo Pharma is showing promise in animal experiments and an early human trial. It could eventually be an alternative or add-on to popular GLP-1 medications.

An experimental obesity pill that works in a different way from the wildly popular Ozempic may help people lose weight, according to results from a small, preliminary human trial.

Ozempic and other GLP-1 drugs reduce food intake by stimulating a feeling of fullness. They act on the brain to promote satiety and on the gut to slow the movement of food through the stomach, helping people feel full longer. As a result, people on the drugs lose weight because they eat less.

But a new drug may be able to burn energy, and thus fat, without reducing appetite. In a Phase I trial described today in the journal Nature Metabolism, the drug led to statistically significant weight loss in participants after two weeks. Dubbed SANA, the drug is derived from salicylate, a compound used to make aspirin. Developed by Eolo Pharma of Montevideo, Uruguay, it activates a pathway called creatine-dependent thermogenesis.

Creatine is perhaps best known as a nutritional supplement taken after exercise to help build muscle mass, but the compound also occurs naturally in the human body and is important for energy production.
“It has been known for a long time that creatine has good effects on metabolism,” says Carlos Escande, cofounder and chief scientific officer of Eolo. In the 1970s, researchers found that rats exposed to cold used a lot of creatine. It wasn’t until a decade ago that a Harvard team found that creatine is used in fatty adipose tissue during exposure to cold to generate heat.

The process of burning energy and generating heat to maintain a stable internal temperature is known as thermogenesis. Creatine-dependent thermogenesis refers to how the breaking down of creatine, particularly in fat cells, contributes to this heat and energy production.

“What we have found is that our compound stimulates this creatine-dependent heat production pathway,” Escande says.

In the first part of the trial, Eolo scientists randomly assigned 17 healthy-weight individuals to receive either a placebo or a single pill of SANA at a low, medium, or high dose. At all doses, the drug was safe and well-tolerated with no serious side effects. In the second part of the trial, they tested the drug in 24 participants with obesity for 15 days. Volunteers were randomly sorted into three groups to receive either a placebo or a low, medium, or high dose of SANA twice a day for the length of the study. Each group had six people taking the drug and two on a placebo. During the study period, participants stayed at a clinical facility where they received high-carbohydrate meals.

At the end of the two weeks, the participants taking the highest dose of SANA showed weight loss of about 3 percent, which is comparable to the weight loss seen in people taking Ozempic and Wegovy over the same period of treatment. They were also asked to fill out a questionnaire regarding appetite and satiety, and none reported decreased appetite or satiety.

While injected GLP-1 drugs are incredibly effective at spurring weight loss, they also come with some downsides. There can be gastrointestinal side effects and loss of muscle mass. The drugs are also expensive, at $1,000 a month or more in the US before insurance. Drug companies are interested in developing anti-obesity pills because of their relatively cheap cost to manufacture compared to injectables, and the fact that some patients would prefer to take a pill.

“There's still an unmet clinical need, and that's where Eolo wants to help,” says María Pía Garat the company’s CEO.

Eolo didn’t exactly set out to make a weight-loss pill. Researchers at the company were originally trying to develop a drug to target inflammation, especially the kind that occurs in obesity and type 2 diabetes. But when they started testing their experimental drug in mice, it not only improved inflammation but also led to a reduction in body weight while they were on a high-fat diet. They have performed experiments out to nine months and found that the mice eventually dropped to their starting weight even while they were still eating the same, high-fat diet.

In mice, SANA also preserved lean muscle mass. MRI scans show that mice treated with SANA had a greater percentage of lean body mass compared to controls, despite substantial fat loss.

“We’ve had stimulants before to try to increase your caloric output,” says Hans Schmidt, chief of bariatric surgery and co-director for the Center for Weight Loss and Metabolic Health at Hackensack University Medical Center, who wasn’t involved in the study.

One of those was the drug combination fenfluramine-phentermine, known as fen-phen, which was sold in the 1990s for weight loss but was taken off the market for causing heart damage. “Those work on overall metabolism. They make you jittery, make you energized. This seems to work specifically at a cellular level on your fat cells,” he says.

Of course, Eolo’s study was very small, and the drug will need to be tested in more people to better understand its effects. The company is planning a Phase II trial later this year that will include around 100 participants with obesity and follow them for 12 weeks. They hope to conduct that trial in the United States. Garat thinks Eolo’s drug could eventually be used as a stand-alone approach or in combination with GLP-1 drugs to produce more weight loss.

✅ Peptides are real and vital to human physiology

⚠️ But others are unregulated, overpromised, or poorly understood — especially in supplement form

“Peptides” aren’t a magic category. They’re molecules.

Ozempic (semaglutide) is a GLP-1 receptor agonist primarily used for managing type 2 diabetes and, in some cases, for weight loss under medical supervision. 

While effective, it has potential negative health effects, which can vary in severity and frequency [permanence]. 

Common Side Effects
These occur in a significant portion of users (often >10%) and are generally mild to moderate:

Gastrointestinal Issues: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain are the most frequently reported. 

Appetite Reduction: While intended for weight loss, excessive appetite suppression may lead to inadequate nutrition or unintended weight loss, especially in non-obese patients.

Fatigue and Dizziness: Users may experience tiredness or lightheadedness, sometimes linked to reduced food intake or dehydration from gastrointestinal effects.

Less Common but Serious Side Effects:
Pancreatitis: Ozempic carries a risk of acute pancreatitis, a potentially life-threatening inflammation of the pancreas. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Immediate medical attention is required.

Gallbladder Issues: Increased risk of gallstones or cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation), particularly with rapid weight loss. Some cases may require surgical intervention.

Kidney Problems: Reports of acute kidney injury or worsening kidney function, often linked to dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea.

Hypoglycemia: In diabetic patients, especially when combined with other glucose-lowering drugs like insulin, Ozempic can cause low blood sugar, leading to shakiness, confusion, or, in severe cases, seizures.

Thyroid Tumors: Animal studies have shown an increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) with GLP-1 agonists, though human risk is unclear. 

Allergic Reactions: Rare but serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis or angioedema, have been reported.

Specific Concerns for Weight Loss Use
When used off-label or in non-diabetic patients for weight loss, additional risks may arise:

Muscle Loss: Rapid weight loss can lead to sarcopenia (loss of muscle mass), which may weaken physical function, especially in older adults.

Nutritional Deficiencies: Prolonged appetite suppression can result in inadequate intake of essential nutrients, potentially causing deficiencies.

Weight Regain: Discontinuing Ozempic often leads to weight regain, sometimes exceeding the initial loss, which can affect metabolic health and mental well-being.

Mental Health Effects: Some users report mood changes, anxiety, or depression, potentially linked to rapid weight changes or physiological effects of the drug. The exact mechanism is not fully understood.

Gastroparesis: Emerging reports suggest a risk of delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis), which can cause severe digestive issues and may persist even after stopping the drug.

Long-Term and Rare[?] Risks
Cardiovascular Effects: While Ozempic generally reduces cardiovascular risk in diabetic patients, some reports suggest potential issues like increased heart rate, which may be concerning for certain individuals.

Cancer Risk: The thyroid cancer risk remains under investigation, and some observational studies have raised concerns about other cancers, though data is inconclusive.

Bone Health: Rapid weight loss may reduce bone density, increasing fracture risk, particularly in postmenopausal women.

Dependency for Weight Loss: Long-term use may be required to maintain weight loss, raising concerns about cost, accessibility, and cumulative side effects.

So when the justice secretary Shabana Mahmood said this week the government was considering compulsory “chemical castration” it was dismissed as juicy red meat lobbed to Reform voters, a distraction from softy stuff like more open prisons and early releases. The UK pilot scheme, which the government will now extend from six to 20 prisons, has shown cuts in recidivism of up to 60 per cent. Another study at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden also revealed remarkable results.

This treatment isn’t appropriate for all sex offenders. Not those who attribute their crimes to drug addiction or who are fuelled by violent rage. But it is effective on paraphiliacs, those driven by an intense sexual fantasy or fixation, which they may feel compelled to act out in real life. Such men are extreme examples of how Sophocles or Socrates — sources vary — described the male libido: “like being chained to a madman”. And many long to be free.

Two types of drugs are used on sex offenders: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) — treatments for depression such as Prozac, which dial down both sex drive and attraction to children. Then there are heavy-duty, testosterone-suppressing anti-androgens, mainly used for prostate cancer: Swedish researchers found that just two weeks after their first injection with degarelix, paedophiles living in the community were less likely to offend. Many reported feeling calm and relief at being untethered from urges which made them dangerous pariahs. Most men asked to continue degarelix after the study ended.

Meanwhile in Florida, injecting paraphiliac sex offenders with the female contraceptive Depo-Provera, often as a condition of receiving probation, has also improved rehabilitation rates.

Sex offenders are devious, manipulative liars, the hardest cons to fix: even Lord Timpson, whose shops are staffed by ex-prisoners, won’t employ them.

What are GLP-1 receptor agonists and what are some common examples? GLP-1 receptor agonists are a class of medications that mimic the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a natural hormone in the body. They were initially developed for managing type 2 diabetes and weight loss. Common brand names include Ozempic (semaglutide), Wegovy (semaglutide), Zepbound (tirzepatide), and Mounjaro (tirzepatide). Tirzepatide is notable because it is a dual agonist, also targeting the GIP receptor.
•
How do GLP-1 receptor agonists work? GLP-1 receptor agonists work by binding to GLP-1 receptors throughout the body. This stimulates insulin secretion in response to high glucose levels, inhibits glucagon release, slows gastric emptying, and can reduce appetite. While their role in glucose metabolism and weight loss is well-established, research and clinical experience suggest they have broader effects due to the widespread presence of GLP-1 receptors, including in the central nervous system, muscles, and various immune cells like mast cells, macrophages, eosinophils, and basophils.
•
Beyond diabetes and weight loss, what other conditions are GLP-1 receptor agonists being used for, particularly in the context of complex illnesses? Beyond their primary uses, GLP-1 receptor agonists are showing promising results, particularly in an off-label capacity, for patients with complex chronic illnesses like Long COVID and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). Clinicians are observing improvements in a wide range of symptoms, including neurological issues (like brain fog and visual disturbances), systemic inflammation, edema, food intolerances, and musculoskeletal pain.
•
Why are GLP-1 receptor agonists potentially effective for conditions like Long COVID and MCAS? One hypothesis is that the efficacy in these complex conditions relates to the presence of GLP-1 receptors on mast cells and other immune cells. By binding to these receptors, the drugs may help stabilize mast cells, reducing the release of inflammatory mediators that contribute to the wide-ranging symptoms seen in these illnesses. The widespread distribution of GLP-1 receptors throughout the body, including in the brain and gut, may also contribute to their systemic effects.
•
Are the effective doses for treating complex illnesses the same as those used for weight loss or diabetes? No, surprisingly, clinicians are finding significant benefits in patients with complex illnesses using much lower doses than those typically prescribed for weight loss or diabetes. These "micro doses" can be as low as one-tenth of the usual starting dose, and patients are experiencing broad symptomatic improvement without significant weight loss, although some initial minor weight loss due to appetite suppression is still possible.
•
What are some observed benefits of using low-dose GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with complex illnesses? Reported benefits in patients on low-dose GLP-1 receptor agonists include significant reductions in inflammation, improved neurological symptoms (like less brain fog), decreased systemic edema, increased tolerance for previously problematic foods, better sleep, and resolution of joint and muscle pain. These improvements are often seen relatively quickly, within a few weeks of starting treatment.
•
Are there any challenges associated with prescribing GLP-1 receptor agonists for complex illnesses? Yes, significant challenges exist. Insurance approval for off-label use in complex illnesses is difficult or impossible, leading patients to rely on compounded versions. However, recent FDA actions regarding declared shortages have impacted the availability of compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide. Additionally, proper dosing with compounded injectables requires careful measurement and conversion by the patient, which can be confusing compared to the more user-friendly pre-filled pens of commercial versions. While commercial versions have known side effects like nausea, clinicians are observing these less frequently at the low doses used for complex illnesses.
•
What is the significance of the widespread distribution of GLP-1 receptors throughout the body? The extensive presence of GLP-1 receptors suggests that these drugs have functions beyond glucose regulation and fat metabolism. This widespread distribution is thought to be key to the observed multi-system benefits in complex inflammatory conditions. It raises questions about the evolutionary purpose of these receptors and how modern diets and lifestyles might be impacting the body's natural GLP-1 system, potentially making exogenous agonists beneficial.

By Amina Niasse

NEW YORK,  May 20 (Reuters) - Online weight-loss company Noom has begun  offering smaller doses of compounded versions of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy as the  U.S. drugs regulator clamps down on mass production of copies of the in-demand  medicine.

Noom will offer its version of compounded semaglutide - the active ingredient  in Wegovy and diabetes drug Ozempic - as part of a program personalized for  patients, which it says will comply with changing U.S. Food and Drug  Administration regulations.

Demand for the new generation of highly effective but pricey weight-loss  drugs has catapulted sales at Noom and rival telehealth sites including Hims  & Hers, WeightWatchers and Ro over the past two years.

Taking small doses of the weight-loss drugs, sometimes referred to as  micro-dosing, has become popular due to the high cost and side effects of the  medicines.

For hundreds of dollars less than the name brand drugs, patients could access  doctors and pharmacy-made versions based on semaglutide or tirzepatide, the main  ingredient in Eli  Lilly's(LLY) rival Zepbound and Mounjaro, due to a regulatory  exception allowing them during drug shortages.

However, the FDA declared the shortages over and its sunset  deadline for compounded versions of Wegovy is May 22.

Noom offers its compounded semaglutide at a starting price of  $149 for the first month. A 2.5 milligram vial of Wegovy or  Zepbound costs $349, according to Novo and Lilly websites.

Analysts have said the telehealth companies must pivot to working with  branded drugs in order to survive after WeightWatchers filed for bankruptcy.

Jeffrey Egler, Noom's chief medical officer, said providers  would determine if patients need a smaller dose because of concerns about  gastrointestinal side effects, or to boost adherence or help keep lost weight  off, for example.

Noom CEO Geoff Cook said the move would not conflict with  regulations. "There is a personalized, and there has always been a personalized,  exception," Cook said.

Novo Nordisk said it is illegal to make or sell semaglutide copies in the  U.S. with only rare exceptions.

"As the FDA has warned, compounders cannot evade federal  compounding laws by selling knockoff semaglutide drugs with manipulated,  unnecessary, and pretextual changes to doses and ingredients," a Novo Nordisk  spokesperson said in a statement.

DOSING

Noom's documents show that a personalized approach could start with half the  typical starter 0.25-milligram dose of Wegovy and gradually increase to about  half the FDA-approved maximum dose of 2.4 mg over 20 weeks.

Medical and Safety Concerns
Side effects like nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are common, particularly at higher doses, and rare but serious risks, such as pancreatitis and kidney issues, raise red flags. A University of Chicago study noted that long-term effects remain understudied, prompting caution, especially for off-label uses like weight loss (GLP-1 Drugs: Effective but Complex). Ozempic (semaglutide) is a medication primarily used for managing type 2 diabetes and, in some cases, for weight loss. Its side effects can range from mild to severe. Below is a comprehensive list based on available medical information:

### **Common Side Effects**
These occur in more than 1% of users and are generally mild:
- **Nausea** (most common, often decreases over time)
- **Vomiting**
- **Diarrhea**
- **Constipation**
- **Abdominal pain**
- **Decreased appetite**
- **Indigestion** or heartburn
- **Fatigue**
- **Headache**
- **Dizziness**
- **Injection site reactions** (redness, itching, or swelling)

### **Less Common but Serious Side Effects**
These are less frequent but may require medical attention:
- **Pancreatitis** (rare but serious; symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, often radiating to the back)
- **Gallbladder problems** (e.g., gallstones or cholecystitis; symptoms include upper abdominal pain, fever, or jaundice)
- **Kidney problems** (worsening kidney function, especially in those with pre-existing kidney issues, often due to dehydration from vomiting/diarrhea)
- **Hypoglycemia** (low blood sugar, especially when combined with other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas; symptoms include shakiness, sweating, confusion)
- **Allergic reactions** (rash, itching, swelling, or difficulty breathing)
- **Increased heart rate**

### **Rare but Severe Side Effects**
- **Thyroid tumors** (medullary thyroid carcinoma observed in animal studies; human risk unclear but carries a boxed warning)
- **Gastroparesis** (delayed stomach emptying, leading to prolonged fullness, nausea, or vomiting)
- **Intestinal blockage** (symptoms include severe abdominal pain, bloating, or inability to pass stool)
- **Vision changes** (worsening or new diabetic retinopathy in some patients)
- **Mental health effects** (rare reports of depression, anxiety, or suicidal thoughts, though causality is not confirmed)

### **Special Considerations**
- **Dehydration risk**: Vomiting or diarrhea can lead to dehydration, which may worsen kidney function.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding**: Not recommended due to potential fetal harm; consult a doctor.
- **Long-term risks**: Ongoing studies are evaluating risks like cardiovascular effects or cancer, but data is limited.

Titled “Acoustic modulation of mechanosensitive genes and adipocyte differentiation,” the study demonstrates how sound, as a non-invasive mechanical stimulus, can alter cellular processes, opening potential avenues for applications in biotechnology and obesity management. 

Background and Motivation
Cells are known to respond to mechanical stimuli through mechanotransduction, a process where physical forces are converted into biochemical signals. 

While previous research has explored high-intensity ultrasound or low-vibration stimuli, the effects of audible sound waves (20 Hz to 20 kHz, within the human hearing range) on cellular behavior have been underexplored due to challenges in isolating sound’s effects from confounding factors like heat or vibrations. 

Kumeta’s team built on their 2018 findings, which showed audible sound could modulate mechanosensitive genes, but sought to refine the experimental setup to directly attribute changes to acoustic waves and investigate their impact on fat cell development.

The researchers designed a precise sound emission system to deliver controlled acoustic waves to cultured cells, minimizing extraneous effects. The setup involved:
•Vibration Transducer: A digital audio player connected to an amplifier sent sound signals to an upside-down vibration transducer mounted on a shelf. This transducer transmitted acoustic waves through a diaphragm to a cell culture dish, simulating physiological sound levels (approximately 100 Pa, comparable to loud conversational or musical sound).
•Sound Patterns: Three sound types were tested: a 440 Hz sine wave (equivalent to the musical note A), a 14 kHz high-frequency tone, and white noise (random broadband sound). These were applied continuously for 2 or 24 hours or in specific schedules for differentiation experiments.
•Cell Types: The study primarily used murine C2C12 myoblasts (muscle precursor cells) for gene expression analysis and 3T3-L1 preadipocytes (fat cell precursors) for adipocyte differentiation studies.
•Analysis Techniques: RNA sequencing identified differentially expressed genes, while microscopy and biochemical assays assessed cellular morphology, differentiation, and molecular pathways. Specific focus was placed on the gene Ptgs2 (prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2, also known as Cox-2) due to its robust response to sound.

The experiments were conducted with controls to ensure sound-specific effects, such as maintaining consistent temperature and minimizing vibrational artifacts. 

For adipocyte differentiation, 3T3-L1 cells were exposed to sound during the initial three-day induction phase with a differentiation medium containing methylisobutylxanthine, dexamethasone, and insulin (MDI), followed by four days in insulin-only medium.

•Non-Invasive Therapies: Since sound is non-material, acoustic stimulation offers a safe, immediate, and non-invasive method to modulate cellular behavior. The study suggests potential for sound-based therapies to manage obesity by inhibiting fat cell formation without drugs or surgery.
•Medical Applications: Beyond obesity, acoustic modulation could guide stem cell differentiation, promote tissue healing, or regulate inflammation, given Ptgs2’s role in these processes. Ozempic (semaglutide) is a medication primarily used to manage type 2 diabetes and, in some cases, for weight loss. Like all medications, it can cause side effects. Below is a concise overview of common and serious side effects based on available information:

### Common Side Effects
These occur in more than 1% of patients and are generally mild to moderate:
- **Gastrointestinal**: Nausea (15-20%), vomiting (5-10%), diarrhea (8-10%), constipation (5-7%), abdominal pain (5-7%), and decreased appetite.
- **Other**: Fatigue, headache, dizziness, and injection site reactions (e.g., redness or discomfort).

### Serious Side Effects
These are less common but require medical attention:
- **Pancreatitis**: Severe abdominal pain that may radiate to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Rare but potentially life-threatening.
- **Hypoglycemia**: Low blood sugar, especially when combined with other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, confusion, or fainting.
- **Kidney Problems**: Worsening kidney function, particularly in patients with pre-existing kidney issues, often linked to dehydration from nausea or diarrhea.
- **Gallbladder Issues**: Gallstones or cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation), with symptoms like upper abdominal pain or jaundice.
- **Allergic Reactions**: Rare but include rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing.
- **Thyroid Tumors**: Animal studies showed an increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Ozempic carries a boxed warning for this risk, though human cases are rare. Avoid in patients with a history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

### Other Considerations
- **Vision Changes**: Some reports of worsening diabetic retinopathy, particularly with rapid blood sugar changes.
- **Heart Rate Increase**: A slight increase in heart rate has been noted in some patients.
- **Mental Health**: Rare reports of mood changes or depression, though not consistently linked.

### Notes
- Side effects are more common when starting treatment or increasing doses. Gradual dose escalation (starting at 0.25 mg weekly) helps reduce gastrointestinal issues.
- Most side effects diminish over time, but persistent or severe symptoms should prompt a consultation with a healthcare provider.
- Always discuss personal risk factors (e.g., history of pancreatitis, thyroid issues, or kidney disease) with a doctor before starting Ozempic.

The open secret in coffee shops, gyms, and beyond, is the widespread use of anti-obesity injections (GLP-1 drugs) even in those who are metabolically healthy and within a normal weight range. While they should be prescribed by a clinician, GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy are increasingly available online on pharmacy and beauty websites, carrying the risk that these products can be counterfeit and poor quality.

GLP-1 drugs work by suppressing appetite: the active ingredient semaglutide mimics the role of a natural hormone called GLP-1 which is produced by our bodies when we eat, and it tells the brain we’ve eaten and makes us feel full. It’s the ‘I’ve had enough to eat’ hormone. 

And yes, semaglutide medications do work to lose weight quickly, but the drugs need to be taken continuously or the weight rebounds. One study found that individuals regained 2/3rds of their weight within a year of stopping medication. In addition, serious side effects affect some patients who take these drugs which is why medical oversight is important. 

The take-away is that while GLP-1 drugs can help those obese or severely overweight to lose weight effectively, lifestyle changes have to happen to sustain these losses. This comes back to exercise and diet as the cornerstones of metabolic health and well-being. 

Part of the problem is our human psychological myopia of worrying about today and tomorrow: you might think you’ll have a salad for dinner but by the time 7pm comes around, the burger and fries option is what you want to eat. Or you’ll plan to go for a 5k jog after work, but then you’re tired and instead do a Netflix binge.

One strategy for getting around this myopia is thinking about what kind of body and life you want to have in 15-20 years. AI visualizations of how you could look at 60 or 70 seem to be effective at getting people to think about their health in a longer-term way. 

For example, a study by Hal Hershfield found that those writing a letter to their future self 20 years older increased daily exercise 1.4x compared to just thinking about a 3-month older future self. I often think about wanting to be independent and active into my 80s, and maintaining fitness and diet towards that goal.

BMI (height/weight metric) is a simple way to capture weight classification and estimate risk of chronic disease. Yet, it can vary dramatically over a year for someone on GLP-1 medication. Insurers have relied on one-off BMI assessments to model health risk, but widespread, off-label use of GLP-1 drugs means that insurers may not even know if someone is taking drugs for short-term weight-loss, and if they are, whether they might stop and the weight will rebound.

The challenge here for health professionals, and insurers, is how to get people to talk about their weight struggles and not feel a stigma about taking GLP-1 drugs over concerns that it could affect the care they get or their health or life insurance premiums. Here’s a breakdown of the benefits:

1. **Enhanced Glycemic Control**:  
   - DPP-4 inhibitors work by blocking the enzyme DPP-4, which breaks down endogenous GLP-1, a hormone that stimulates insulin secretion and suppresses glucagon release in a glucose-dependent manner. This increases natural GLP-1 levels modestly.
   - GLP-1 receptor agonists, on the other hand, directly mimic GLP-1 and provide a more potent and sustained activation of GLP-1 receptors.
   - Together, they amplify insulin secretion and reduce blood glucose levels more effectively than either alone, without significantly increasing the risk of hypoglycemia since their actions are glucose-dependent.

2. **Complementary Mechanisms**:  
   - DPP-4 inhibitors increase the body’s own GLP-1 levels, while GLP-1 agonists provide an external, supraphysiological dose of GLP-1-like activity. This dual approach targets the incretin system more robustly.
   - GLP-1 agonists also slow gastric emptying and promote satiety, effects that are less pronounced with DPP-4 inhibitors alone, adding an extra layer of glucose regulation and potential weight management.

3. **Weight Management Benefits**:  
   - DPP-4 inhibitors are generally weight-neutral, meaning they don’t cause weight gain or loss.
   - GLP-1 agonists often lead to weight loss due to their appetite-suppressing effects and delayed gastric emptying.
   - Combining them can result in modest weight loss (from the GLP-1 agonist) without the risk of weight gain that might occur with other diabetes medications like sulfonylureas or insulin.

4. **Low Risk of Hypoglycemia**:  
   - Both classes work in a glucose-dependent manner, meaning they primarily enhance insulin release and suppress glucagon when blood sugar is elevated. This reduces the likelihood of dangerously low blood sugar compared to treatments like insulin or sulfonylureas.

5. **Improved Beta-Cell Function**:  
   - Preclinical and clinical studies suggest that both DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists may help preserve or improve pancreatic beta-cell function over time, which is critical in type 2 diabetes where beta-cell decline is a key issue.

6. **Cardiovascular and Other Benefits**:  
   - Some GLP-1 agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits, such as reduced risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk patients.

This combination is often considered when metformin alone isn’t enough to achieve glycemic targets, or in patients who need additional control without the side effects of other drugs (e.g., hypoglycemia or weight gain). Studies, such as those published in journals like *Diabetes Care* and *The Lancet*, have shown that combining these agents can lower HbA1c (a measure of long-term blood sugar control) more effectively than monotherapy, often by an additional 0.5–1.0% depending on the specific drugs and patient factors.

### Practical Example
A patient might take a DPP-4 inhibitor like sitagliptin (e.g., Januvia) daily in pill form alongside a weekly GLP-1 agonist injection like dulaglutide (e.g., Trulicity). New study finds weight loss drugs could increase the risk of hair loss | Kristen Dalli, Consumer Affairs

Semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, is being called into question

Several studies have been done on the myriad list of side effects that come from popular weight loss drugs.

A new study conducted by researchers from the University of British Columbia have looked at the impact of these drugs on hair loss. According to their findings, semaglutide, the active ingredient in both Wegovy and Ozempic, was associated with an increased risk of hair loss.

“Anecdotal data has alluded to hair loss as another adverse event associated with semaglutide,” the researchers wrote in the report. “Data from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have reported more hair loss events with GLP-1 agonists compared to other antihyperglycemics.

“However, to date, no epidemiologic study has examined this association in a real-life clinical setting, especially in those taking semaglutide purely for weight loss.”

The study

The researchers analyzed data from the IQVIA PharMetrics Plus for Academics database, which included information on 16 million people.

For the purposes of this study, all of the participants selected were first-time semaglutide users. None of the participants had been diagnosed with diabetes or had a history of taking similar drugs.

The study included nearly 2,000 people taking semaglutide, and compared the results with over 1,300 people taking a similar drug with a different active ingredient – bupropion-naltrexone.

The researchers followed the participants’ health outcomes from the time they were prescribed the weight loss drugs through the time they were diagnosed with hair loss.

The results

Ultimately, those taking semaglutide were more likely to experience hair loss than those taking bupropion-naltrexone. Additionally, women taking semaglutide were more likely than men to experience hair loss.

The researchers hypothesized why this relationship between semaglutide and hair loss may exist:

Rapid weight loss may increase physiological stress, which can increase the risk of hair loss. Semaglutide has been linked with more rapid weight loss than bupropion-naltrexone, which could explain the greater likelihood of hair loss.

Semaglutide helps users lose weight by suppressing the appetite; however, with a lower appetite, those taking the drug may also not be getting the vitamins and nutrients necessary for healthy hair growth. Similarly, those experiencing gastrointestinal issues – like vomiting – as a result of semaglutide may not be retaining the vitamins and nutrients they need for healthy hair growth.

It’s also possible that semaglutide users experience hormone dysregulation, which can also impact hair growth.

While the researchers believe more research is needed in this area, they encourage consumers to consider these side effects before beginning treatment.

Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists have demonstrated significant improvements in glycemia, adiposity, and cardiovascular outcomes. However, their benefits may be overstated, and side effects underreported. This perspective piece examines the efficacy, sustainability, and financial implications of GLP-1RA therapies, exploring the necessity of integrating alternative strategies such as lifestyle modifications and therapeutic carbohydrate reduction.

In recent years, the treatment landscape for obesity and type 2 diabetes has been significantly transformed by the introduction of glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). These pharmacological agents are designed to enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon secretion, suppressing appetite and slow gastric emptying, thereby improving glycemic control and promoting weight loss. Originating from the incretin hormone concept, GLP-1RAs have not only shown promising results in clinical trials but also received widespread acclaim for their ability to improve cardiovascular outcomes and reduce adiposity.
Despite these advancements, a critical examination of the real-world application of GLP-1RAs reveals a more nuanced picture. The initial enthusiasm driven by controlled clinical environments often does not fully translate into everyday clinical practice, where a variety of factors influence drug efficacy and patient adherence. This perspective paper aims to critically analyze the outcomes of major GLP-1RA trials, juxtaposing these findings with real-world data to highlight significant challenges in side effects management, cost, and long-term sustainability of benefits. Furthermore, it discusses the need for a comprehensive approach that integrates alternative and adjunctive strategies, such as lifestyle modifications and dietary interventions, particularly therapeutic carbohydrate reduction, to manage obesity and type 2 diabetes more effectively and sustainably.
The increasing reliance on GLP-1RAs also raises important questions regarding their long-term impact on health and economics. Recent data suggests a disparity between the outcomes observed in tightly controlled trial settings and those achieved in broader clinical practice. For example, while trial results have shown substantial efficacy in weight reduction and glycemic control, real-world studies indicate high discontinuation rates due to adverse effects and diminishing returns over time. Additionally, the economic burden posed by high-cost biopharmaceutical treatments like GLP-1RAs necessitates a critical examination of their cost-effectiveness, especially when compared to non-pharmacological interventions.
This introduction sets the stage for a thorough review of the literature surrounding GLP-1RA therapies, aiming to elucidate their true value in the management of chronic metabolic diseases and to explore viable alternative approaches that may offer equal or greater efficacy at a lower cost and with fewer side effects.

STEP Trials Analysis
The STEP (Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with obesity) clinical trials have been pivotal in demonstrating the efficacy of semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, in weight management. The STEP trials, particularly notable for their rigor and scale, reported that semaglutide significantly reduces body weight by enhancing feelings of satiety and reducing appetite. However, a closer examination reveals critical nuances. While the average weight loss observed was substantial, approximately 25% of participants achieved less than a 5% reduction in body weight over 104 weeks. This finding is particularly significant as a 5% weight reduction is often considered clinically relevant for improving metabolic health outcomes in obese individuals.
Moreover, the efficacy in suppressing appetite appeared to diminish over time. By week 104, cravings and hunger levels in some participants rebounded to levels comparable to those observed with placebo, suggesting a potential decrease in the drug's effectiveness or an adaptation by the body to the medication.

Adverse events reported in the STEP trials, particularly gastrointestinal issues, were frequent and severe enough to warrant discontinuation for some patients. The STEP 5 trial noted an 82.2% incidence of gastrointestinal side effects, which raises substantial concerns about the tolerability and long-term usability of semaglutide. Such high rates of adverse effects highlight a significant barrier to adherence and sustained use, questioning the practicality of long-term therapy with GLP-1RAs.

SURMOUNT Trials Insights
Parallel to the STEP trials, the SURMOUNT trials assessing tirzepatide highlighted similar challenges. While tirzepatide demonstrated significant initial weight loss, these trials also underscored the sustainability issues post-therapy. Notably, many participants regained weight after discontinuing the medication, indicating that while effective during active treatment, GLP-1RAs might not provide a lasting solution to obesity management.

SCOPE Trial and Other Observations
The SCOPE trial and other observational studies in real-world settings have shown that the effectiveness of GLP-1RAs appears diminished outside of controlled trial environments. A notable finding across several studies is a high discontinuation rate, often exceeding 50%, primarily due to adverse effects. Additionally, concerns have been raised about the quality of weight loss, with a significant proportion stemming from lean muscle mass rather than fat mass. This kind of weight loss can impair metabolic health further and increase the risk of mortality.

Health Risks and Cost Implications
While GLP-1RAs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide have shown promising results in improving glycemic control and reducing weight, their long-term health implications warrant careful consideration. One of the more concerning potential side effects is an increased risk of certain types of cancers, notably thyroid cancer. Data from several long-term studies and post-marketing surveillance have indicated a statistically significant correlation between prolonged use of GLP-1RAs and elevated rates of thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents, though the relevance of these findings to human risk is still under investigation.
Additionally, the high incidence of gastrointestinal side effects can not only affect quality of life but also lead to nutrient malabsorption and potential deficiencies. These side effects are often the primary reason for discontinuation, as observed in multiple real-world studies, thus limiting the long-term utility of these treatments.

Economic Burden of GLP-1RA Therapies
The financial implications of widespread GLP-1RA use are substantial. With annual costs per patient ranging from $6,000 to $9,000 for newer agents like semaglutide, the projected economic burden on healthcare systems could potentially reach upwards of $600 billion annually if these therapies were to be adopted broadly across the eligible patient population in the United States alone. This figure does not account for the additional costs associated with managing side effects and monitoring long-term health risks.
The cost-effectiveness of GLP-1RAs, particularly when compared to non-pharmacological interventions such as lifestyle modification and dietary adjustments, raises significant concerns. While these medications offer notable short-term benefits, their long-term value is diminished by high costs, potential health risks, and the necessity of indefinite treatment to maintain weight loss and metabolic improvements.

Comparing Costs to Alternative Treatments
When considering alternatives like intensive lifestyle interventions, which may include dietary changes, regular physical activity, and behavioral therapy, the cost disparity becomes even more pronounced. Studies have shown that such interventions can yield substantial improvements in weight and metabolic health at a fraction of the cost of GLP-1RA therapies. For example, therapeutic carbohydrate reduction has been documented not only to reduce weight but also to improve glycemic control and reduce or eliminate the need for diabetes medications in some patients.
These economic considerations are crucial for policymakers and healthcare providers as they balance clinical benefits with sustainability and affordability in healthcare planning.

Emphasizing Lifestyle Modifications
The limitations of pharmacological interventions such as GLP-1RAs highlight the critical need for integrated treatment approaches that include significant lifestyle modifications. Intensive lifestyle interventions (ILIs), which encompass a range of activities from dietary changes to increased physical activity and behavioral therapy, have been shown to be effective in achieving sustainable weight loss and improving metabolic health.
For instance, structured exercise programs and tailored health coaching can lead to substantial improvements in cardiovascular fitness, glycemic control, and overall well-being. These programs also promote a higher level of patient engagement and adherence compared to drug therapies, as they empower patients to take an active role in managing their health. Moreover, the community support aspect of many lifestyle programs can provide the motivational reinforcement necessary to maintain these healthier habits long term.

The Role of Dietary Adjustments
Particularly relevant to this discussion is the role of dietary interventions, such as therapeutic carbohydrate reduction (TCR). TCR involves lowering intake of refined sugars and starches and has been documented to improve glycemic control and reduce insulin levels in patients with type 2 diabetes. Unlike GLP-1RAs, which generally require ongoing treatment, dietary changes can lead to durable metabolic improvements and potentially reduce or eliminate the need for medications.
Several studies have compared the efficacy of dietary approaches to pharmacological treatments, finding that well-formulated low-carbohydrate diets not only foster weight loss but also enhance lipid profiles and reduce inflammation. These benefits make TCR a compelling, cost-effective alternative to GLP-1RA therapy, particularly for patients who prefer to avoid long-term medication use.

Integrating Approaches for Comprehensive Care
While no single approach will be suitable for every patient, the integration of pharmacological treatments with lifestyle and dietary modifications offers a promising pathway forward. For some patients, initiating treatment with GLP-1RAs might be necessary to achieve rapid metabolic stabilization, but transitioning to a maintenance strategy focused on lifestyle changes could be more sustainable and beneficial in the long run.
Collaborative care models that include dietitians, physical therapists, and behavioral health specialists working alongside medical providers can tailor interventions to meet individual patient needs. This model not only addresses the physiological aspects of obesity and diabetes but also considers the psychological and social factors contributing to these conditions.

The review of glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) in the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes has illuminated several critical issues. While GLP-1RAs have shown promise in clinical trials, offering substantial improvements in glycemia, weight reduction, and cardiovascular outcomes, their real-world applicability is hampered by significant challenges. These include adverse side effects, high costs, and a lack of long-term sustainability. Moreover, the potential health risks associated with long-term use of these agents, such as an increased risk of certain cancers, necessitate careful consideration and monitoring.
The economic implications of widespread GLP-1RA usage are profound, with potential costs running into hundreds of billions annually, a financial burden that may not be justified by the long-term outcomes of these treatments. This economic evaluation underscores the need for more cost-effective, sustainable, and patient-friendly treatment options.

Alternative approaches, particularly intensive lifestyle interventions and therapeutic carbohydrate reduction, have shown considerable promise in not only managing but potentially reversing the effects of obesity and type 2 diabetes. These strategies emphasize the importance of diet and exercise, which can lead to sustained improvements in health without the ongoing costs and side effects associated with pharmacological treatments. Furthermore, the integration of lifestyle modifications alongside or in place of drug therapies offers a more holistic approach to disease management, which can be tailored to individual needs and preferences, thereby enhancing adherence and long-term success.

Future research should focus on long-term comparative studies between pharmacological treatments and lifestyle interventions to provide clearer guidance on the most effective, sustainable, and cost-effective methods for managing chronic metabolic diseases. Additionally, more research is needed to explore the psychological and social factors that affect patient adherence to lifestyle changes, as these are crucial for the success of non-pharmacological interventions.

It is imperative for clinicians, researchers, and policymakers to collaborate in reassessing the role of GLP-1RAs and considering the potential of holistic approaches that prioritize patient well-being and long-term health. This reassessment should aim to integrate more comprehensive care models that consider not only the metabolic symptoms but also the lifestyle and psychological factors contributing to obesity and type 2 diabetes.

As we advance, the medical community must embrace these integrated approaches, ensuring that all patients have access to effective, affordable, and patient-centered care that addresses the complexities of their conditions with dignity and respect.

A podcast by the ever-popular Oprah Winfrey — where she interviewed endocrinologist Dr Ania Jastreboff from Yale University — emphasised the concept of #obesity as a disease. A recent Lancet commission report on obesity also said the same. Just to put the record straight, the WHO classified obesity as a disease in 1997. In fact, not only is it a disease like diabetes or hypertension, it is also the mother of most chronic diseases, requiring lifelong management.

The word “obesity” carries a stigma and it can be highly demotivating for an individual to be labelled obese or morbidly obese, terms that are widely used. A reasonable suggestion by the American Association of Endocrinologists, which we have adopted, is the acronym ABCD — Adiposity Based Chronic Disease.

Regardless of the semantics, we have to think of obesity as a chronic “neuroendocrine” disease — a disturbance of the hormone-brain axis. When we eat, the intestines send out signals (like the GLP1 hormone) to the pancreas and other parts of the body, including the brain. The brain tells us when we are satiated and should stop eating. Brain centres, under the influence of brain hormones, also control our appetite. Putting it simply, dysregulation of this hormone-brain axis leads to a mismatch between our requirements and what we eat. As a result, we eat excessively and put on weight. This axis determines the set point for weight and is different for every individual. Very often, therefore, it is not the individual’s fault that they tend to gain weight more easily than their peers, or lose less weight than others on medication.

If we think of obesity as a disease, we will have little problem in accepting that it should be treated with medication. There is no reason for feeling guilty or ashamed about the use of medication to treat obesity. It is not a sign of defeat. We need to think of obesity in the same way as we think of other chronic diseases like diabetes, blood pressure and high cholesterol. The new class of GLP1 drugs typified by semaglutide (#ozempic , #Wegovy) and tirzepatide (#Mounjaro, #Zepbound) — and a whole bunch of new ones in development — at least partially treats the biological defect in the brain that causes obesity. By resetting the set point, they help us lower weight. However, as with most medications, they work only as long as they are used. Once off the drug, the weight can come back. The method for dose adjustment that I use is similar to that discussed by Dr Jastreboff. The principle is to start low and increase slowly, to reduce side effects. When target weight has been achieved or weight has plateaued at the maximum tolerated dose, I try to continue the patient on the lowest possible maintenance dose.

It is very important to set realistic targets when initiating therapy. The target cannot always be what the patient desires. A conversation about this between patient and doctor is essential. For someone who is 5’8” and weighs 120 kg, to aim for an ideal body weight of 70 kg is virtually impossible. It is important not to be driven by cosmetic considerations alone. Many individuals have body image issues — I get requests from women who are underweight but want to lose more weight for a modelling assignment or a wedding. It is also important for potential users to realise that not everyone loses huge amounts of weight.

While obesity is a disease, it cannot be treated just by medication. One can never ignore that treating obesity involves a lot of effort on the individual’s part, and lifestyle measures remain the foundation of successful management — in the same way as for diabetes. I have some patients who tend to depend solely on medication and stop making any lifestyle effort. Such patients are bound to be long-term failures as they will gain weight rapidly whenever they try to reduce the medication dose.

There was not much discussion about side effects in the Oprah interview, but I would like to point out some. Gastro-intestinal side effects are common and usually manageable. Pancreatitis is exceedingly rare. Muscle loss that occurs due to rapid weight loss, although not a direct drug effect, is of particular concern among Indians who often have low muscle mass to start with. The recent report of the rare occurrence of eye optic neuropathy (NIAON) with the use of semaglutide tells us that continued pharmacovigilance is required. And while it is true that most patients with obesity require continued treatment, I would be cautious in recommending lifelong treatment with the new GLP1 drugs for every obese individual till more data emerges.

These reduce hunger signals but are often used short-term due to potential side effects like increased heart rate.

Drugs like Atorvastatin and Ezetimibe target obesity-related conditions like high cholesterol rather than directly addressing weight loss.

Naturally occurring molecule rivals Ozempic in weight loss, sidesteps side effects | Krista Conger, Stanford Medicine

A naturally occurring molecule identified by Stanford Medicine researchers appears similar to semaglutide — also known as Ozempic — in suppressing appetite and reducing body weight. Notably, testing in animals also showed that it worked without some of the drug’s side effects such as nausea, constipation and significant loss of muscle mass.

The newly discovered molecule, BRP, acts through a separate but similar metabolic pathway and activates different neurons in the brain — seemingly offering a more targeted approach to body weight reduction.

“The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues,” said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. “That’s why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism.”

Svensson has co-founded a company to launch clinical trials of the molecule in humans in the near future.

Svensson is the senior author of the research, which was published March 5 in Nature. Senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD, is the lead author of the study.

The study would not have been possible without the use of artificial intelligence to weed through dozens of proteins in a class called prohormones. Prohormones are biologically inert molecules that become active when they are cleaved by other proteins into smaller pieces called peptides; some of these peptides then function as hormones to regulate complex biological outcomes, including energy metabolism, in the brain and other organs.

Each prohormone can be divided in a variety of ways to create a plethora of functional peptide progeny. But with traditional methods of protein isolation, it’s difficult to pick peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) out of the biological soup of the much more numerous natural byproducts of protein degradation and processing.

The researchers focused on the prohormone convertase 1/3, which separates prohormones at specific amino acid sequences and is known to be involved in human obesity. One of the peptide products is glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1, which regulates appetite and blood sugar levels; semaglutide works by mimicking the effect of GLP-1 in the body. The team turned to artificial intelligence to help them identify other peptides involved in energy metabolism.

Peptide Predictor

Instead of manually isolating proteins and peptides from tissues and using techniques like mass spectrometry to identify hundreds of thousands of peptides, the researchers designed a computer algorithm they named Peptide Predictor to identify typical prohormone convertase cleavage sites in all 20,000 human protein-coding genes. They then focused on genes that encode proteins that are secreted outside the cell — a key characteristic of hormones — and that have four or more possible cleavage sites. Doing so narrowed down the search to 373 prohormones, a manageable number to screen for their biological effects.

“The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings,” Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor predicted that prohormone convertase 1/3 would generate 2,683 unique peptides from the 373 proteins. Coassolo and Svensson focused on sequences likely to be biologically active in the brain. They screened 100 peptides, including GLP-1, for their ability to activate lab-grown neuronal cells.

As expected, the GLP-1 peptide had a robust effect on the neuronal cells, increasing their activity threefold over control cells. But a small peptide made up of just 12 amino acids bumped up the cells’ activity tenfold over controls. The researchers named this peptide BRP based on its parent prohormone, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

When the researchers tested the effect of BRP on lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do) they found that an intramuscular injection of BRP prior to feeding reduced food intake over the next hour by up to 50% in both animal models. Obese mice treated with daily injections of BRP for 14 days lost an average of 3 grams — due almost entirely to fat loss — while control animals gained about 3 grams over the same period. The mice also demonstrated improved glucose and insulin tolerance.

Behavioral studies of the mice and pigs found no differences in the treated animals’ movements, water intake, anxiety-like behavior or fecal production. And further studies of physiological and brain activity showed that BRP activates metabolic and neuronal pathways separate from those activated by GLP-1 or semaglutide.

The researchers hope to identify the cell-surface receptors that bind BRP and to further dissect the pathways of its action. They are also investigating how to help the peptide’s effects last longer in the body to allow a more convenient dosing schedule if the peptide proves to be effective in regulating human body weight.

“The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades,” Svensson said. “Nothing we’ve tested before has compared to semaglutide’s ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans.”

GLP-1, or Glucagon-Like Peptide-1, is a hormone produced in the gut, primarily by the L cells of the small intestine, in response to food intake. It plays a key role in regulating blood sugar levels and appetite. Here’s a breakdown of what it does:

Blood Sugar Control: GLP-1 stimulates insulin secretion from the pancreas in a glucose-dependent manner, meaning it helps lower blood sugar when levels are high (like after a meal). It also suppresses glucagon release, a hormone that raises blood sugar by prompting the liver to release stored glucose.

Appetite Regulation: It slows gastric emptying (how fast food leaves the stomach) and signals the brain to increase feelings of fullness, which can reduce food intake.

Other Effects: It has cardiovascular benefits, like reducing inflammation and improving heart function, and may protect pancreatic beta cells (which produce insulin).

These drugs mimic GLP-1’s actions, amplifying its effects.

Gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying) is not the main mechanism through which GLP-1RA drugs lead to weight loss; indeed, it's mostly transient.

Human and animal evidence speaks to this fact.

In one trial, participants were randomized to receive either once-weekly semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) or a placebo, like so:

To measure whether Semaglutide led to differences in gastric emptying, the authors provided everyone with standardized meals and paracetamol (acetaminophen/Tylenol) and then take blood samples to see how rapidly the paracetamol is absorbed into the blood. This is an indirect method of measuring gastric emptying, but it works very well, as assessed by the gold standard method, scintigraphy.

But I digress. The result of the study is that people ate less, and at twenty weeks, there was no medically-significant difference in gastric emptying for people in the placebo or semaglutide groups. To quote:

"The AUC0–5h,para was 8% higher in the s.c. semaglutide 2.4 mg group compared with the placebo group at week 20 (estimated treatment ratio [ETR] 1.08; P = 0.0054). The difference in AUC0–5h,para between groups was no longer statistically significant when adjusted for body weight at week 20 in a post hoc analysis (ETR 1.05; P = 0.1218)."

What they found is, thus, that there was a minimal difference in gastric emptying, and it might even be attributable to differences in bodyweight. Since the groups people were in were assigned randomly, and it makes sense to adjust this for bodyweight given its theoretical relevance (and it's a simple adjustment!), it seems likely there's really no difference of any import in humans.

But we even know that this same finding shows up in animals, and the fact that it does can be used to explain the measure I just referenced in the human study--AUC, Area Under the Curve. What curve? The paracetamol concentration over time. In the first administration, rats not on GLP-1RAs--in this case, liraglutide--had far slower gastric emptying, and you can see this because it takes them a long time to process all that paracetamol. Look at the curve:

But after fourteen days of continuous use of liraglutide, you'll notice that the curve is practically indistinguishable from the one for the placebo. 

Per the authors, "These data indicate that regulation of appetite signals in the brain, and not GE, is the main mechanism for liraglutide-induced weight loss."

The vast majority of people taking weight-loss drugs like Wegovy or Ozempic quit within two years. A new study surveyed more than 120,000 people, with and without type 2 diabetes, who were taking a GLP-1 medication.
